lessons.title: Cash & Cash Flow
lessons.description: Why cash keeps a business alive, how it differs from profit, and how to read a cash-flow forecast.
lessons.content_html:
Cash Keeps a Business Alive

A business can be profitable on paper and still collapse if it runs out of cash. Wages, rent and supplier bills all have to be paid in actual money on the day they fall due — the tax office and the landlord do not accept IOUs. Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over time. If more is going out than coming in for too long, the business becomes insolvent and folds.

This is why the single biggest trap in GCSE Business is assuming profit and cash are the same thing. A sale generates profit the moment it is made, but the cash may not arrive for 30, 60 or 90 days if the customer is on trade credit. Meanwhile the business still has to pay wages every Friday.

Key Fact

Profit is not the same as cash. A profitable business can still fail if cash is not available to pay wages, rent and suppliers on the day they are due. Profit measures the whole trading year; cash is about day-by-day timing.

Why Cash Provides Liquidity

Liquidity means having enough cash ready to meet short-term debts and expenses — the VAT bill, the supplier invoice due on Friday, the wages on the 28th. A liquid business has cash on hand or money coming in that can be used immediately. An illiquid business may be wealthy on paper (lots of stock, lots of customers owing money) but still unable to pay a £500 bill today.

This is why most sensible managers keep a cash reserve — a cushion large enough to cover a couple of months of outflows. It prevents one late payment from becoming a crisis.

Reading a Cash-Flow Forecast

A cash-flow forecast is a table that predicts cash in and cash out, month by month. OCR expects you to interpret one and to complete missing cells — you will not have to build one from scratch. The four key rows are:

Cash inflows — money coming in from sales, loans, new investment or asset sales.

Cash outflows — money going out on wages, rent, stock, utilities, loan repayments.

Net cash flow — inflows minus outflows for that month. It can be positive or negative.

$$\text{Net cash flow} = \text{Total inflows} - \text{Total outflows}$$

Opening and closing balances — the opening balance is how much cash the business had at the start of the month. The closing balance is opening balance + net cash flow, and it becomes next month’s opening balance.

Worked Example — Completing a Forecast

A Cornish surf shop’s forecast shows some cells filled in and others blank. January opening balance is £8,000. January inflows are £12,000 and outflows are £15,000. February inflows are forecast at £10,000 and outflows at £11,000. Complete the missing cells.

Step 1 — January net cash flow:

$$\pounds12{,}000 - \pounds15{,}000 = -\pounds3{,}000$$

Step 2 — January closing balance:

$$\pounds8{,}000 + (-\pounds3{,}000) = \pounds5{,}000$$

Step 3 — February opening balance is January’s closing balance: £5,000. February net cash flow: £10,000 − £11,000 = −£1,000. February closing balance: £5,000 + (−£1,000) = £4,000. The shop ends February with £4,000 — still positive, but the trend is downwards. If March repeats the same shortfall the balance will drop to £3,000 and the shop will need action.

Key Fact

Closing balance = Opening balance + Net cash flow. Net cash flow = Cash inflows − Cash outflows. The closing balance of one month becomes the opening balance of the next.

Why Cash-Flow Forecasting Is Useful

A forecast is a planning tool. It anticipates periods of cash shortage before they hit, so the owner has time to arrange remedies — negotiate longer supplier credit, arrange an overdraft, chase unpaid invoices. It also provides targets: if the forecast shows January inflows of £12,000 the owner knows to hit that or act fast. Dunelm, the UK homeware retailer, faces a predictable seasonal pattern — spring and summer peaks, quieter autumn. Forecasting lets it plan stock purchases and supplier payments so cash stays positive year-round.

Causes and Fixes for Cash-Flow Problems

Problems come from a handful of common causes: overspending on stock or equipment, slow-paying customers, seasonal sales dips, or growing too fast so outflows race ahead of inflows. When a forecast shows a shortfall, a manager has four main levers.

Re-scheduling payments — negotiate longer trade credit with suppliers or delay non-urgent bills. Low cost, but can damage supplier relationships if overused.

Arrange an overdraft — a short-term bank facility for a dip. Quick and flexible, but interest is high and the bank can withdraw the facility at short notice.

Reduce cash outflow — cut non-essential spending, renegotiate rent, switch to cheaper suppliers, hold less stock. Takes time to bite but has no borrowing cost.

Increase cash inflow — chase unpaid invoices, offer discounts for early payment, run a promotion. The right fix for overdue debtors, but promotions can squeeze profit margins.

The right fix depends on the problem. A one-off dip — a major customer paying two weeks late — is what overdrafts are designed for. A structural problem — outflows consistently higher than inflows — cannot be fixed by borrowing, because the debt just grows. That needs cost cutting, price changes or new revenue streams.
lessons.exam_tip_html: OCR will not ask you to construct a whole cash-flow forecast, but you WILL be asked to complete missing cells and interpret the result. For ‘Calculate’ and ‘Complete’ questions, show the working (inflow − outflow, or opening balance + net cash flow) even when the answer is easy — method marks are credited even if your final number is slightly off. For ‘Analyse’ and ‘Discuss’ questions on cash flow, chain your reasoning: explain WHY a negative closing balance threatens survival, not just that it does. Always name the business in the stem when applying.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cash is not the same as profit. A profitable business can still fail if it cannot pay wages, rent or suppliers on time.
  • A cash-flow forecast shows inflows, outflows, net cash flow and opening/closing balances month by month. Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow.
  • Cash-flow problems can be fixed by rescheduling payments, arranging an overdraft, reducing outflows or increasing inflows — each with a different cost and risk.

lessons.title: Ethical & Environmental Considerations
lessons.description: How ethics and environment shape business decisions — and the trade-offs with profit.
lessons.content_html:
Doing the Right Thing — at a Price

When Primark found in 2013 that a factory in Bangladesh it bought clothes from had collapsed, killing more than a thousand workers, it faced a choice: keep paying the lowest price for garments or spend more to audit suppliers and improve conditions. When BrewDog set a 2030 carbon-negative target, it agreed to invest heavily in land restoration and renewable energy. These are classic examples of ethical behaviour — doing what stakeholders consider fair and honest, even when it costs more.

Key Fact

Acting ethically usually raises costs — higher wages, better-sourced materials, environmental clean-up — but can also raise revenue and loyalty by winning customers who care. An OCR answer will always weigh both sides.

Treatment of Workers

Ethical treatment of workers covers pay, safety, hours, and dignity at work. Paying above the legal minimum wage raises staff costs but often cuts turnover and training bills. John Lewis pays a share of profits to all staff (called ‘partners’) — the scheme has run since 1929 and is one of the reasons staff retention is so strong. In 2020 Boohoo was accused of buying from Leicester suppliers paying far below the minimum wage; sales fell, the share price dropped, and the company had to commission an independent review.

Treatment of Suppliers

Businesses choose how hard to push the firms that supply them. Ethical treatment means paying a fair price, paying on time, and checking that suppliers themselves are not using unsafe conditions or modern slavery. Tony’s Chocolonely, the Dutch chocolate brand sold widely in UK supermarkets, was founded in 2005 after journalist Teun van de Keuken discovered child and forced labour in West African cocoa supply. Tony’s buys directly from farmer cooperatives at a premium above market price and traces every bean — a genuinely slavery-free supply chain. Big supermarkets that delay supplier payments by 60 or 90 days often face legal and reputational challenge for squeezing small farmers.

Treatment of Customers

Ethical treatment of customers means honest advertising, safe products, clear terms, and genuine after-sales support. In 2015 Volkswagen was caught fitting ‘defeat devices’ to hide the true emissions of its diesel cars — the dieselgate scandal cost the firm over thirty billion dollars in fines and lost sales, and damaged its brand for years. Consumers punish firms that mislead them, and regulators increasingly back them up.

Sourcing of Materials and Marketing Decisions

Ethical sourcing means choosing raw materials from suppliers who meet ethical and environmental standards — Fairtrade coffee and chocolate, certified sustainable timber, cotton that is not picked by forced labour. It also means saying no to cheap options that fail those tests. Costa Coffee and Greggs both sell only Fairtrade coffee in their UK cafes, accepting the higher cost in exchange for credibility with customers.

Ethical marketing means not targeting vulnerable groups (gambling adverts around children’s TV), not exaggerating product claims, and being honest about ingredients and origins. The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority fines firms that get this wrong.

The Ethics-Versus-Profit Trade-off

A trade-off is when a business must give up something in one area to gain in another. Paying a UK living wage raises staff costs — but can cut staff turnover and build brand reputation. Switching to recyclable packaging raises material costs — but can attract new customers and avoid future regulation. Sometimes the ethical choice is profitable long-term: Patagonia, the outdoor brand, built its entire identity on environmental responsibility (it famously ran a ‘Don’t Buy This Jacket’ ad) and grew faster than rivals. But in the short run, ethical choices can hit profits and test shareholders’ patience.

Pressure groups and consumers amplify unethical behaviour fast. Greenpeace campaigns have forced tuna brands to switch to pole-and-line fishing to protect dolphins; PETA campaigns have pushed cosmetics firms to stop testing on animals. Social media means a single factory-scandal video can reach millions before a PR team drafts a response.

The message is clear: unethical shortcuts can generate short-term profit, but when media, regulators or customers find out, the long-term cost usually outweighs the gain.

Environmental Considerations

Every business decision has an environmental footprint. Operations generate traffic congestion (think of Amazon vans on every street), noise and air pollution, and waste that ends up in landfill. Consumers, councils and governments increasingly expect businesses to act. Supermarkets charge for carrier bags; Starbucks and Pret offer discounts for reusable cups; Deliveroo is testing electric bikes and cargo cycles for last-mile deliveries.

Sustainability means meeting today’s needs without using up resources future generations will need. The UK’s net-zero target has pushed firms into electric vans, energy-efficient buildings and carbon offsets.

Waste disposal: recycling is now a standard cost. Costa Coffee runs cup-recycling schemes; Tesco takes back soft plastic at its stores. Pollution: vehicles in UK clean-air zones like London’s ULEZ pay daily charges. Climate change: sourcing, transport and packaging all generate carbon — McDonald’s has committed to sourcing fish only from certified sustainable fisheries and beef from farms with reduced methane emissions, protecting its future supply chain while cutting the impact today.

Costs and Benefits of Ethical and Green Behaviour

Costs include higher-priced raw materials, staff training on new procedures, investment in cleaner technology, and the risk of greenwashing — claiming green credentials without genuine action. Customers and regulators are quick to spot and punish this.

Benefits include stronger brand reputation, the ability to charge premium prices, better staff retention, and early compliance with future laws. When governments later tighten rules, ethical firms do not need to scramble. Ethics and sustainability are no longer optional — they shape what materials a firm uses, how it hires, what it claims in adverts, and how quickly it can react when a new law lands.

Key Fact

Environmental impacts of business activity include traffic congestion, noise and air pollution, waste sent to landfill, and the use of scarce resources. Sustainable practices aim to reduce each of these without shutting the business down.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Ethics questions almost always reward a balanced answer — do not just write ‘being ethical is good’. For ‘Analyse’ questions, build a chain of reasoning: ‘recyclable packaging raises material costs, which squeezes margin, but attracts eco-conscious customers, which lifts revenue.’ For 12-mark ‘Evaluate’ or ‘Recommend’ questions, the judgement must introduce a weighting — for example, ‘it depends on the customer base’ — not just repeat the points above. Always name a real example where you can, and apply every point to the business in the stem.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ethical behaviour covers treatment of workers, suppliers, customers, sourcing of materials and marketing decisions — every area carries a cost and a reputational benefit.
  • Environmental considerations include sustainability, waste disposal, pollution and climate change — firms that act early avoid later fines and protect supply chains.
  • Every ethical choice is a trade-off between short-term cost and long-term reputation; a balanced OCR answer names both and applies them to the business in the case study.

lessons.title: The Economic Climate & Globalisation
lessons.description: How changing income, unemployment and globalisation affect UK businesses at home and abroad.
lessons.content_html:
The Economic Climate Affects Every Business

No business operates in a vacuum. When wages rise, people buy more; when unemployment climbs, they cut back. The economic climate is the broader state of the UK economy, and its two key moving parts for OCR are changing levels of consumer income and unemployment. Both shape what customers can spend, what businesses can sell, and what they have to pay for staff and stock.

Changing Levels of Consumer Income

When take-home pay rises faster than prices, customers have more disposable income. They eat out more, replace older phones sooner, book holidays, and trade up to premium brands. When disposable income falls — as it did across the UK during the 2023 cost-of-living squeeze, when food and energy prices jumped ahead of wages — customers do the opposite. They cut restaurant visits, switch from M&S to Aldi, repair rather than replace, and delay big purchases.

Impact on businesses varies sharply by what they sell. Luxury brands (Burberry, Fortnum & Mason) are hit hard in a squeeze because their products are the first thing customers drop. Value brands (Aldi, Primark, Wilko in its heyday) often grow in a squeeze because shoppers trade down. Essential-goods businesses (Tesco, utility firms) are more stable because people still buy food and heat homes.

Key Fact

Rising consumer income lifts demand for luxury and non-essential goods; falling income shifts demand towards value brands and essentials. The same economic shock produces opposite winners and losers.

Unemployment

Unemployment is the number of people actively looking for a job but unable to find one. High unemployment has three effects on UK businesses. First, customers with no wages spend less — so sales fall across non-essential sectors. Second, wage costs drop because more people compete for each job, which can ease hiring costs for firms that are still growing. Third, government spending on benefits rises, which can translate into higher business taxes later to pay for it.

Low unemployment has the opposite effect. Customers spend confidently, but businesses face recruitment pressure: fewer applicants per job, higher wages, and real difficulty filling skilled roles. The UK hospitality sector struggled badly after Brexit and the pandemic as restaurants and hotels fought each other for chefs and waiters, with many putting up pay 10–20% to attract staff. Recession makes the opposite problem bite.

Through 2022 and early 2023 UK food prices rose at around 17–19% year-on-year — the fastest rise in forty years. Energy bills doubled. Wages rose more slowly, so real disposable income fell. Pub chain Wetherspoon saw sales wobble as customers ate at home instead; Greggs saw sausage-roll sales rise as shoppers traded down from sit-down lunches; Aldi overtook Morrisons to become the fourth-largest UK supermarket. The same economic squeeze rewarded cheap and punished expensive.

It also reshaped costs. Cafés and restaurants watched the price of flour, eggs, cooking oil and electricity climb each month. Some passed the rise on in higher menu prices; others absorbed it and watched margins thin. A few closed entirely because they could not do either fast enough.

What Globalisation Is

Globalisation is the process by which national economies have become more connected — trade flows, investment, people and ideas moving more easily across borders. For UK businesses it means three big things: access to foreign customers, access to cheaper imports, and far more competition from abroad.

Growth of Multinationals

A multinational is a business that operates in more than one country. Apple, Unilever, Nestlé, Samsung, Amazon and Toyota all sell in the UK but are based abroad. Multinationals bring jobs (Nissan’s Sunderland plant employs 7,000 people), investment (Amazon has built UK warehouses in Tilbury, Manchester, Coventry) and tax revenue — but they also squeeze smaller UK rivals. Independent bookshops struggled when Amazon undercut them on price; independent electronics retailers closed when Currys and Amazon dominated the market.

International Branding and Competition

Globalisation lets successful UK brands sell worldwide. Dyson sells vacuums and fans in 80 countries; BrewDog opened bars in Berlin, Sao Paulo and Tokyo. International branding means keeping a consistent name, look and product worldwide — the Coca-Cola logo looks the same in Manchester and Mumbai. It costs more upfront (translation, local adaptation, shipping) but builds huge global recognition.

Globalisation also means UK businesses compete with firms they would never have met twenty years ago. A small British t-shirt printer now competes with Chinese firms shipping direct via Temu and Shein. A UK software start-up competes with Indian developers charging a fraction of UK rates.

Global supply chains let UK businesses buy cheaper components, finished goods and labour abroad. Dyson designs in Malmesbury but manufactures in Malaysia; many UK supermarkets source fresh produce from Spain and Morocco; UK call centres have been offshored to India and the Philippines for decades. This keeps prices down for UK customers — but when a global supply chain breaks, every firm that depends on it is hit.

The 2021 supply chain crisis proved it. A combination of Covid factory closures, a shortage of shipping containers, blockage in the Suez Canal (the Ever Given) and HGV driver shortages meant UK businesses waited months for parts and stock. Car production stalled across Europe because of a missing computer-chip supply from Taiwan. Empty supermarket shelves appeared across the UK. Globalisation cuts costs — but it also concentrates risk in far-away bottlenecks.

Influences on Location

Globalisation changes where businesses choose to operate. A UK car firm may build its factory in a country with lower labour costs; a software firm may hire developers in Poland or India remotely; Dyson moved its headquarters to Singapore in 2019. Nissan chose Sunderland in the 1980s because the UK offered easy access to the EU single market — and had to reconsider after Brexit added export paperwork. Multinationals pick locations based on costs, skills, tax, trade deals and proximity to customers — all now chosen across the whole planet, not just one country.

Key Fact

Globalisation gives UK businesses access to bigger markets and cheaper imports — but exposes them to stronger international competition and supply-chain shocks that start thousands of miles away.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Economic-climate questions reward specific examples over generic answers. Name an actual UK business and an actual event (the 2023 cost-of-living squeeze, the 2021 supply chain crisis) — markers credit real application far more than textbook phrasing. For ‘Discuss’ and ‘Evaluate’ questions, remember both winners and losers: a recession hurts Burberry but boosts Aldi, so a good answer names both. You do NOT need to calculate interest rate changes or exchange rate conversions — those are not in the OCR spec. Focus on qualitative impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rising consumer income lifts demand for luxury and non-essential goods; falling income shifts demand to value brands and essentials — the same shock rewards and punishes different businesses.
  • High unemployment cuts customer spending but eases hiring costs; low unemployment boosts spending but forces wages up and makes recruitment hard.
  • Globalisation gives UK businesses bigger markets and cheaper imports but also more competition and exposure to far-away supply-chain shocks.

lessons.title: The Interdependent Nature of Business
lessons.description: How operations, finance, marketing and HR connect — the synoptic skill Paper 2 tests.
lessons.content_html:
A Business Works as One System

Every business has four main functions — operations, finance, marketing and human resources — and none of them works alone. A decision in one area ripples straight into the others. Launch a new product and marketing needs to know who the customer is, operations needs to know how to make it, finance needs to know what it will cost and what it will earn, and HR needs to know what skills the team needs to deliver it. This is the interdependent nature of business, and it is the single biggest idea the final part of the OCR course asks you to carry into the exam.

The lesson also introduces how financial information measures and explains performance, and how risk and reward weaves through every decision. A well-prepared student will not just describe each function separately — they will show how the functions connect.

Key Fact

The four business functions — operations, finance, marketing and HR — are interdependent. A decision in any one function affects all the others, which is why every major business decision has to be planned across the whole firm, not in one department alone.

Worked Example — Greggs Launches the Vegan Sausage Roll

In January 2019 the UK bakery chain Greggs launched a vegan sausage roll nationwide. It became the fastest-selling product in the company’s history, made the front pages, and helped push annual sales up by 7.4%. Behind the headline launch sat months of co-ordinated work across every function. Follow it through and every interdependence becomes visible.

Marketing — Spotting the Opportunity

Marketing started with research. Veganuary, a UK campaign encouraging people to try plant-based eating for January, had grown tenfold between 2015 and 2018. Greggs saw a clear customer demand its current menu did not serve. Marketing built the positioning (a product as close to the original sausage roll as possible) and planned the release date to catch Veganuary. It also built the famous “vegan sausage roll in an iPhone box” media teaser, which generated free press coverage worth far more than the paid budget.

Operations — Making It Work

Operations had to solve a real problem: create a sausage-roll substitute that tasted and cooked the same as the meat original, using Quorn as the filling, in factories that had always handled pork. The recipe had to be shelf-stable for daily delivery to 1,900 shops. Supply chain had to be scaled so the new product launched on day one in every shop — not just London. Stock levels had to anticipate demand that marketing was deliberately stoking up.

Finance — Funding and Forecasting

Finance modelled the cost: new ingredients, new packaging, new adverts, possible losses if the product flopped. It worked out a price that covered costs and left a margin; it set a sales forecast that let operations know how much to produce; it made sure there was cash to pay Quorn and the new suppliers before customers started buying. If finance had underestimated demand and run out of cash for ingredients, the launch would have stalled halfway through January.

HR — Training and Communication

HR had to train thousands of shop staff on the new product — why it was vegan, how to heat it, how to answer customer questions. It had to brief managers on the media interest, because Greggs shops would suddenly be on the news. In some stores, HR had to adjust rotas to cope with the surge in lunchtime footfall. None of this was visible to customers, but without it the launch would have been chaos on day one.

Picture each function acting alone. If marketing had launched the campaign without warning operations, the product would have sold out on day one — damaging brand trust. If finance had refused the budget, marketing could not have booked adverts. If HR had not trained staff, customers would have faced confused service. If operations had not scaled factories, shelves would have been empty. Every function enables the others. A successful launch is a system, not a department.

Risk and Reward in Every Decision

Every cross-function decision balances risk and reward. Greggs could have stuck with its existing menu — zero launch cost, zero risk — but also zero share of the growing vegan market. By launching, it accepted real risks: the product might flop, factories might struggle, customers might reject the change. The reward was huge if it worked. In the event, it worked. But the decision had to be made before the outcome was known — that is what every business leader faces.

Risk and reward is not just about new products. Every pay rise, every supplier change, every store closure balances an upside against a downside. A good answer recognises this in the case-study business in front of you, not as a separate theory.

How Financial Information Measures Performance

Financial information is how a business checks whether interdependent decisions are working. Financial information includes revenue, costs, profit and loss, gross and net margins, average rate of return, and cash flow figures. Greggs measured the vegan launch through sales data (did the forecast hold?), cost data (did production come in on budget?), profit margin (did the pricing work?), and cash flow (did the firm stay liquid through the launch surge?).

Financial information is the feedback loop. Marketing may claim the campaign worked, but only finance can confirm how the figures moved. Operations may say production ran smoothly, but only cost data confirms whether the promised margin held. Without financial information to measure outcomes, the four functions cannot tell what is working or where to adjust next.

Key Fact

Synoptic questions on the synoptic section of the final paper ask you to link content from the whole course. Work through all four functions in turn, connect each to risk and reward, and use any financial information in the stimulus to support your judgement.

How OCR Synoptic Questions Are Framed

the synoptic section of the final paper includes at least two synoptic questions. These are usually extended-response Discuss, Evaluate or Recommend questions worth 9 or 12 marks. The stimulus typically gives you a business facing a decision — opening a new branch, launching a product, switching supplier, entering a new market — plus numbers (a cash flow extract, a break-even figure, a margin, a sales target). To score full marks you need to:

Step 1 — Identify at least two functions involved. Do not answer from only one. A new branch involves operations (site, staff) AND finance (cost, cash) AND marketing (local awareness) AND HR (hiring). Name the functions explicitly.

Step 2 — Link them. Do not list separately. Show how the finance decision enables the operations plan and how marketing success depends on HR training. The word ‘because’ is your friend.

Step 3 — Use the numbers. If the stimulus gives a break-even figure, margin or cash balance, use it in your reasoning. Marks are left on the table when candidates ignore the data.

Step 4 — Make a supported judgement. Recommend questions need a clear decision. Weigh one side against the other and justify your answer in the specific context — ‘it depends on X’ is acceptable only if you justify which value of X would change the decision.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Synoptic questions reward breadth plus linkage. Walk through all four functions even if the question names one — examiners credit you for showing how a finance decision depends on an HR or operations input. Always use any numbers in the stimulus; a qualitative answer on a case study with figures is capped below the top band. For ‘Recommend’ questions make a decision — not a summary. For ‘Discuss’ and ‘Evaluate’ questions, the judgement should weigh one factor over another with a clear because-clause, not just restate the points above.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Operations, finance, marketing and HR are interdependent — a decision in one ripples through all four.
  • Every business decision balances risk and reward, and financial information is the feedback loop that tells managers whether the decision is working.
  • Synoptic questions on Paper 2 expect you to link content from the whole course — name multiple functions, link them, use the data, and commit to a supported judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which financial information supports decision making across a business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a use (e.g. measuring whether a marketing campaign worked, checking production costs, monitoring cash, judging a price change).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘sales and margin figures show whether the price supported by marketing is producing enough profit’.
3 marks: applies to a business outcome — e.g. ‘so managers can decide whether to extend the campaign, cut costs in operations, or change the price before the next quarter’.
Indicative answer: ‘Financial information like sales and margin figures (1) shows managers whether a marketing promotion is covering its cost and adding profit (2), which lets them decide whether to extend the campaign or pull it before more money is wasted (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a decision to launch a new product affects three different functions within a UK business. (Context: a mid-sized UK cereal brand has approved a new plant-based granola range for launch in six months. The board wants to know how the launch will affect operations, finance and HR.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked chains, one per function, each tracing the launch to a concrete business impact. Operations: new ingredient supply, factory line changes, quality testing → cost and capacity pressure. Finance: upfront cost, cash flow during ramp, margin target, break-even for the new range. HR: training, possible new hires, rotas around launch. Links between functions explicit. Sustained context.
Secure: Two or three functions with developed chains and clear linkage.
Developing: Functions named but chains short or weak.
Emerging: Lists tasks without chains or application.
Indicative content: operations → new production line → extra cost + risk of quality issues; finance → funding ramp → cash flow squeeze before sales arrive; HR → train staff + possibly hire → wage bill up. Generic answers without reference to the UK cereal brand cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a small UK café chain should open two new branches this year. (Context: a café chain with five branches in Bristol has £150,000 in retained profit. The owner is considering opening two more branches. Forecast ARR for each new branch is 22%; forecast break-even for each is 800 customer visits a week; each branch would need three new staff and a marketing launch.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated synoptic answer linking at least three functions (operations: site set-up, supply; finance: use of retained profit, ARR, break-even; marketing: local awareness; HR: hire and train six staff) with two-sided reasoning, explicit use of the numbers (22% ARR, 800 weekly break-even, £150,000 available), a supported judgement weighed for this specific chain — e.g. ‘open one branch first, prove the model, then open the second; 22% ARR beats any alternative investment, but spreading £150,000 across two simultaneous launches leaves no cushion if break-even slips’.
Secure: Clear balanced argument, three functions named, numbers used, judgement applied to the chain.
Developing: Partial linking, some function depth, weak use of numbers, basic judgement.
Emerging: One-sided or generic; lists points without weighing.
Indicative content: reward — 22% ARR beats savings rates, growth builds brand; risk — 800 visits/week break-even is steep for a new branch, £150,000 split across two leaves no emergency cash, HR load of hiring six trained staff simultaneously. Judgement options: open one then the second, open both, delay both, franchise instead. Generic answers without reference to the Bristol chain or the numbers cannot score above 6. [12 marks]
